Lane's catalogue raisonné identifies the foreground of ⟦0⟧Ten Pound Island, Gloucester⟦1⟧ as George Rogers's wharf on Fort Point, with the island at center and Eastern Point beyond; Erik Ronnberg aligned the viewpoint on the 1865 Harbor Commissioners' chart.⟦2⟧ For ⟦3⟧Ship in Fog⟦4⟧ the catalogue puts Lane in the channel “just off Fort Point.”⟦5⟧ The 1847 Thyssen picture was taken from a little higher and farther back, near Duncan's Point.
The catalogue calls the light of ⟦0⟧Ten Pound Island⟦1⟧ “the hazy light of a late summer afternoon,” in apricot hues.⟦2⟧ ⟦3⟧Ship in Fog⟦4⟧ is early morning, the summer sea fog burning off in stages.
The island and harbor mouth are unchanged in outline, but Fort Point's 1850s wharves are gone, and the tower Lane painted (1821) was replaced in 1881.
We could not confirm public shore access on Fort Point itself. Ten Pound Island is also visible across the water from a public way on Rocky Neck.
For the Lane effect, go in late August, about two hours before sunset; for the fog picture, a still June or July morning.

In summer 1880 Homer boarded on Ten Pound Island with the lighthouse keeper, Oliver Merrill.⟦0⟧⟦1⟧ Princeton places ⟦2⟧Eastern Point Light⟦3⟧ in the series “painted by Homer on Ten Pound Island.”⟦4⟧ Where on the island he sat is not recorded; the line on the map runs from the island's light to Eastern Point Light, almost due south.

Eastern Point Light⟦0⟧ is a moonlit night: rapid blue washes for the sky, the full moon “scraped out,” the water dappled by gouging with the brush end.⟦1⟧ Most of the series are sunsets over the western shore;⟦2⟧ in early August the sun sets in the west-northwest, to the painter's right when facing the harbor mouth.
The island is owned by the City of Gloucester, which keeps walking paths to the light; private boaters may land, but there is no landing facility. The tower itself is Coast Guard property and closed.
Without a boat, paint the island and Homer's sunsets from the Rocky Neck public way, looking west across the harbor.
Homer's 1880 method, per the MFA: let paint soak into the paper, blot it out, then lay on thick opaque dashes.
Site 3 of 9 · Willard Metcalf and Childe Hassam

Banner Hill is the ridge above Smith Cove, from which “many of the most notable American impressionist landscapes of Gloucester were painted.”⟦0⟧ Metcalf's ⟦1⟧Gloucester Harbor⟦2⟧ was “painted from Banner Hill looking westward”; Hassam's 1899 view was taken from the same hill, “a little farther to the left” than Duveneck's.⟦3⟧⟦4⟧ The marker is the hill's road (OpenStreetMap); the exact spots are not recorded.

Metcalf painted “with the morning sun at the artist's back,” so the town across the harbor is lit full-face.⟦0⟧ At 9 a.m. in early August the sun stands in the east, about 36° up, behind and to the right of a painter facing downtown.
The Banner Hill vantage is now private property and not open to the public; the view can be seen from the road.
Go in the morning. In the afternoon the town is backlit and the harbor turns to glare.
Rocky Neck's Art Trail marks this and other historic painting sites.

Lane's source drawing is inscribed “Brace's Rock, Eastern Point / F.H. Lane del. / Aug. 1863” and lists five buyers for paintings made from it. The catalogue says he drew from “the coast just north of the cove,” not the beach.⟦0⟧ The marker is the nearest shore point north of the cove (MassGIS); the exact spot is not recorded. Duveneck painted the same rock about 1893.⟦1⟧ From the marker the rock lies south-southeast; because the Terra Foundation describes Lane's view as looking east across the cove, he may have stood farther west along the shore.

The Terra Foundation describes the view as looking east across the cove, “the unseen sun in the west” tinting the far rocks pink while the foreground lies in shadow: late afternoon.⟦0⟧ One version shows autumn foliage, so Lane varied the season.
In Lane's day the cove was part of the private Niles Farm, with Niles Pond between it and the harbor.⟦0⟧ We could not verify public shore access today.
Go late in the afternoon with the sun behind you, and watch the far rocks turn warm in the last hour.
Lane worked from a measured drawing, then painted several near-identical canvases from it. Make the drawing on site and the painting at home.

Lane “drew the rock from the shore looking to the south” in 1861, on a drawing gridded for transfer; the boat drifts in the cove just north of the rock. The catalogue includes a viewpoint chart.⟦0⟧ The marker is the nearest shore point north of the cove (MassGIS).

A newspaper in 1862 called it “a sunset scene”: the sky moves from purple at upper left to coppery yellow at right, the light of early twilight.⟦0⟧ Facing south, the setting sun is off to the right (west), which is where Lane put his brightest sky.
The rock lies a few hundred feet offshore and can be reached over the rocks at low tide; at high tide it is an island.⟦0⟧ Mind the tide: the harbor range averages nearly 9 feet.
OpenStreetMap shows a Normans Woe Wildlife Sanctuary along this shore; we did not verify its access rules.
Go for the last half hour before sunset, and keep the sky warm on the right and cool at upper left, as Lane did.

The back of the canvas reads “View of Coffin's Beach, from the rocks at the Loaf, after a sketch taken, August, 1862.” Ronnberg plotted the viewpoint, and MFA staff concluded Lane used a camera lucida, then widened the scene in the painting.

Dawn: an 1862 notice says the sun is just rising behind the hills, in pink-to-blue light.⟦0⟧ At sunrise in early August the sun comes up in the east-northeast, nearly straight down the line of view, so the scene is backlit.
The Two Penny Loaf is mapped as a nature reserve (OpenStreetMap); we did not verify access to Coffin's Beach.
Be in place before sunrise (5:34 a.m. on August 1, 2027) and paint the first 20 minutes.
A camera lucida, or a phone photo traced the same way, is a fair modern stand-in for Lane's method.

A secondary source describes ⟦0⟧Horizon at Gloucester⟦1⟧ as the port's skyline “from Eastern Point.”⟦2⟧ The marker is placed at Eastern Point Light; the exact spot is not recorded. Duveneck stayed at the Harbor View Hotel in East Gloucester.

From Eastern Point the city lies almost due north, about 3.8 km away, so the sun is behind or beside the painter all day and the skyline is always lit from the front: from the east in the morning, the south at midday, the west in late afternoon.
The lighthouse is Coast Guard property and closed to the public.⟦0⟧ The Dog Bar Breakwater beside it is a 2,250-foot granite jetty: wear sturdy shoes and stay off it when waves break over the stones.
Duveneck's foreground is low-tide ledge and weed. Time a session for low water and the tide pools will give you his foreground.

The title places the picture at Lighthouse Beach beside Annisquam Light, on Wigwam Point.⟦0⟧ Jones's exact spot is not recorded, and the museum page could not be checked for it. The line on the map is a modern alternative: the light can be seen from Wingaersheek Beach across the river mouth.
No source describes the time of day. From Wingaersheek you look north at the light: morning sun is side-lit from the right, and afternoon sun comes over your left shoulder onto the tower.
The light's keeper's house is Coast Guard housing; the light can be viewed from Wingaersheek Beach.
Non-resident beach parking must be reserved in summer (Memorial Day to Labor Day).
Jones's sand and ledge change with the tide. At low water the flats here widen a great deal.

Twachtman painted ⟦0⟧Harbor View Hotel⟦1⟧ “from the end of the long pier,” the hotel's float on Wonson's Cove, looking back at the hotel with his cottage studio at far left. It was on his easel when he died there in August 1902.⟦2⟧ The hotel stood at what is now 21 Eastern Point Road.⟦3⟧ The pier's end is placed at the middle of the cove.
Not described in the sources. Facing the hotel from the cove is roughly an eastward view, so late-afternoon sun would fall full on the buildings from behind the painter.
The hotel is gone; the site is Rocky Neck Art Trail stop 15, reached on foot from Rocky Neck Avenue.
The painting is at the Nelson-Atkins Museum (33-57). Its image is not reproduced here, so look at it on the museum's page before you go.

Field notes: palettes, light, conditions and four painting days
The practical pages of the guide in one place. The pigment lists are suggestions for today's tube colors, not a record of what each painter used. ⟦0⟧The color lab is in the interactive guide.
In the spirit of Fitz Henry Lane · Oil
Glassy water, an apricot haze low in the sky, rocks and hulls nearly in silhouette.
Lay the sky first in one sitting: warm and light at the horizon, cooler and a little darker toward the top. Blend until no brushmark shows.
Paint reflections with vertical strokes, a shade darker than the sky they mirror. A single horizontal wipe makes the water lie flat.
Keep the darkest values for the near shore and boat hulls. Everything past the middle distance stays close to the sky's value.
Lane worked from careful pencil studies. A quick, accurate line drawing of the shore is time well spent.
In the spirit of Winslow Homer, 1873 & 1880 · Watercolor
Fast transparent washes, white paper left for sails and glints, a few bold opaque accents.
Wet the sky and drop color in, then leave it. Lifting with a damp brush or tissue gives you clouds and moonlight.
Reserve the white of the paper for sails, gulls and sparkle. Masking fluid is a modern shortcut; Homer mostly painted around them.
The MFA describes his 1880 method: let paint soak into the paper, blot it out, then add thick opaque dashes. Try it on a test sheet first.
Sit low on the shore so the horizon falls in the upper third and the boys, dories and pots read against the water.
In the spirit of Childe Hassam and Willard Metcalf · Oil
Broken color, bright mid-morning light, shadows painted in blues and violets instead of black.
Leave black off the palette. Mix shadow color from ultramarine, rose and a touch of the local color.
Set dabs of pure color side by side and let them mix in the eye, especially on water and foliage.
Mid-morning side light, around 9 to 10 a.m. in summer, gives the strong color and modeling these painters favored on Banner Hill.
Work on a mid-value warm ground so the bright notes sing and the gaps don't read as glaring white.
In the spirit of John Twachtman · Oil
Close, chalky values and a muted, limited palette. Atmosphere over detail.
Mix three or four piles of value before you start and paint only from them.
Thin paint, scrubbed and scumbled, keeps the surface dry and matte like pastel.
Overcast days and late-afternoon haze suit this palette. Leave the sunny postcard view for another day.
Squint constantly. If two shapes are the same value, paint them the same value.
In the spirit of Maurice Prendergast · Watercolor & gouache
Crowds, umbrellas and boats turned into flat, jewel-like dabs of color.
Draw in color, not pencil: outline figures with a fine brush, then fill them in flat.
Repeat each color three or four times around the sheet to knit the picture together.
Busy beaches and harbor days, such as Good Harbor Beach or the Fiesta waterfront, give plenty of subjects.
In the spirit of Edward Hopper and Stuart Davis · Oil or watercolor
Clapboard houses, strong cast shadows, simplified shapes and flat color.
Design the shadows first. Morning or late-afternoon sun throws long shadow shapes across the houses of East Gloucester and Rocky Neck.
Simplify: one value for the sunlit wall, one for the shadow side, one for the sky.
Paint buildings from public sidewalks. Don't set up in front of someone's door or driveway.
About 30 minutes before sunrise or after sunset
Cool, shadowless light and quiet water. Lay in the big shapes quickly; the light changes minute by minute.
The Atlantic side of Cape Ann faces east. Low sun rakes across the granite and backlights the surf.
Clear side light and full color. Banner Hill looking over Smith Cove works well now, as it did for Metcalf and Hassam.
Flat, overhead light with small shadows. A good time for museum visits, drawing, or painting under an umbrella in the shade.
Warm haze over the harbor, still water, long reflections. The Lane catalogue calls the light of Ten Pound Island the hazy light of a late summer afternoon.
From Rocky Neck and Ten Pound Island the sun goes down behind the western shore of the harbor. Homer painted a series of these sunsets in 1880.
Most common on calm late-spring and early-summer mornings
Fog flattens values and swallows distance. Lane's Ship in Fog shows it burning off in stages. Paint the near shapes dark and let everything else dissolve.
Homer's Eastern Point Light is a moonlit night. Work small, with a headlamp on a red setting, and judge colors the next morning.
Gloucester's mean tidal range is about 8.8 feet. Ledges, weed lines and mudflats appear and vanish within an hour or two, so check the tide table and choose your tide the way you choose your light.
Afternoon sea breezes are common in summer. Weight your easel, clip down paper and canvas, and keep a brick-sized stone or a hook for your bag.
Wet, weedy rock at Brace's Cove, Eastern Point and Halibut Point is treacherous. Set up above the high-water line and never turn your back on the surf.

Summer brings haze and crowds. September and October bring clear air, lower sun and fewer people; Cape Ann Plein Air takes place in early October. Winter light is low and golden all day, with the sun setting far to the southwest.

In Massachusetts much of the shore between high and low water is privately owned, and the public right there is limited to fishing, fowling and navigation. Paint from public ways, beaches and parks, or ask permission.
Beach lots charge seasonal fees and fill early on summer weekends. Rocky Neck and Bearskin Neck have little parking; walk or use the Cape Ann Transportation Authority buses.

A minister’s wife from Sterling, Massachusetts, Mellen came into Fitz Henry Lane’s world after her brother-in-law took the Universalist pulpit in Gloucester in 1855. By the middle of the decade she was working beside Lane, with free use of his drawings and at times his canvases; one painting, ⟦0⟧Coast of Maine⟦1⟧, carries both their signatures⟦2⟧. Her ⟦3⟧Field Beach, Stage Fort Park⟦4⟧, about 1850, shows this shore and is at the Cape Ann Museum⟦5⟧; Bowdoin owns her ⟦6⟧Gloucester Harbor (Laying Nets)⟦7⟧⟦8⟧.

The museum owns Theresa Bernstein’s ⟦0⟧Gloucester in Blue⟦1⟧ (1925)⟦2⟧, Nell Blaine’s ⟦3⟧Wharf Studio, Gloucester⟦4⟧ (1958)⟦5⟧ and the archive of the Folly Cove Designers⟦6⟧; the Rocky Neck Art Colony also credits it with Martha Walter’s ⟦7⟧Rocky Neck Store and My Studio⟦8⟧ (1920)⟦9⟧. In the summer of 1923 Jo Nivison painted ⟦0⟧Church Towers, Gloucester⟦1⟧, a head-on view of this church’s twin towers. It was the summer she and Edward Hopper painted together here, and she encouraged him to take up watercolor⟦2⟧. We have not found the painting in a public collection.

The three painters’ summers here are the subject of ⟦0⟧Avery, Gottlieb & Rothko: By the Sea⟦1⟧, shown at the Cape Ann Museum in 2026⟦2⟧ and at the Phillips Collection in Washington from October 24, 2026, to January 24, 2027⟦3⟧. A sketch in his notebook shows the footbridge at Bass Rocks by Good Harbor Beach, a subject Leon Kroll had painted before him⟦2⟧.

The harbor in the paintings was a factory. This page explains what the painters were looking at — fish flakes, dories, schooners, nets — and where the working waterfront can still be seen.
Low wooden racks on which split, salted cod was laid out in the sun to dry. Whole fields of them appear in Lane’s and later paintings of the waterfront⟦0⟧.
Nets hung like a curtain in the water, catching fish by the gills. Mellen’s ⟦0⟧Gloucester Harbor (Laying Nets)⟦1⟧ shows crews setting them⟦2⟧.

Small flat-bottomed boats carried on the schooners and rowed out to set lines and nets; Gordon Parks photographed Gloucester crews laying nets by hand from them in 1943⟦0⟧. Homer drew boys in dories in 1873.

Sea smoke forms when very cold air moves over water that is much warmer than it, usually when the air is below about 10°F. The water evaporates and condenses at once into fog that rises in columns⟦0⟧. Look for it on the first still, clear morning after an Arctic cold front, just after sunrise, from Stacy Boulevard or the Rocky Neck causeway.

Lane painted the harbor frozen in the 1850s. Aldro Hibbard, who taught in Rockport, painted it under snow; the Museum of Fine Arts bought his ⟦0⟧Winter Days⟦1⟧ in 1920⟦2⟧, and the Smithsonian American Art Museum owns his ⟦3⟧Rockport Winter⟦4⟧⟦5⟧.
Oil paint keeps working in the cold; watercolor and acrylic freeze. If you use water media, work small and fast and keep the water in a vacuum flask.

Cape Ann was photographed by some of the century’s best: the government’s documentary photographers in the 1930s and 1940s, and Aaron Siskind, who found abstraction on its wharves. None of these photographs is reproduced here; each link goes to the museum or library that holds it.

Siskind came in July 1944 to a studio Adolph Gottlieb had found for him, and spent his mornings on the wharves and beaches with a camera and tripod. In Gloucester he turned from documentary work to close, flat views of peeling walls, rope, a discarded glove and granite. His painter friends Gottlieb, Barnett Newman and Mark Rothko encouraged him⟦0⟧. The curator Jan Howard called these summers his breakthrough⟦1⟧.
Try it⟦0⟧Paint as he looked: pick a square meter of a wharf wall, a stack of traps or a weathered door, and fill the whole picture with it.
1943, for the Office of War Information

Parks photographed Gloucester’s fishing families at home and went to sea with the crew of the ⟦0⟧Alden⟦1⟧, who laid their nets by hand from dories. The assignment was part of a wartime project on food production⟦2⟧. The photographs are in the Library of Congress.
Rothstein photographed the fishing boats and docks in the fall of 1937; prints are in the New York Public Library and the Library of Congress⟦0⟧.
Friedlander photographed the city in 1981; the Museum of Modern Art owns ⟦0⟧Gloucester, Massachusetts⟦1⟧ of that year⟦2⟧.
Chiarenza, later Siskind’s biographer, photographed in Gloucester as a young man; the Whitney owns his ⟦0⟧Gloucester Window, Sailing Ship⟦1⟧ of 1962⟦2⟧.

The painters of Cape Ann: their lives here and who brought whom

Cape Ann’s painters arrived by invitation more often than by chance. A teacher brought his class, a friend found a cottage, an older painter asked two young ones to come for the summer. These are their lives on Cape Ann, and the chains that brought them.
Read each chain left to right: each painter brought, taught or welcomed the next. Names link to the profiles below.

Gloucester’s own painter learned his trade in the lithography shops before turning to oil, and came home to paint the harbor for two decades⟦0⟧. The Cape Ann Museum holds 40 of his paintings, his first known work (a watercolor of 1830), about 100 drawings and all three of his lithographed views of the town⟦1⟧. He worked from careful measured drawings, then painted several canvases from each; see site 4.
Working with Lane from the mid-1850s

Born in Vermont and schooled in watercolor at a girls’ academy, Mellen married a Universalist minister in 1840. When his brother took the Gloucester pulpit in 1855, she came into Lane’s orbit and was soon working beside him, free to copy his drawings and sometimes his canvases. One painting carries both signatures. The museum notes she is often called a “copyist”, and that Lane plainly respected her work⟦0⟧.

Hunt brought the French Barbizon painters’ ideas to Boston and taught John La Farge and both William and Henry James. His summer studio in Magnolia drew other artists to Cape Ann, and from 1868 he opened his classes to women, many from Boston’s leading families⟦0⟧.

Homer left the studio in Gloucester. In 1873 he painted outdoors and made himself a master of watercolor, almost to the exclusion of oil; in 1880 he boarded on Ten Pound Island in the middle of the harbor⟦0⟧. Both summers are on the guide’s map as sites 1 and 2.

In 1890 the Kentucky-born painter brought a summer class of students from Boston and the Cincinnati Academy, apparently the first large class of its kind in town, and he went on to paint about a hundred Gloucester pictures⟦0⟧. He drew others after him, among them Theodore Wendel, Joseph DeCamp, John W. Alexander and John Twachtman. He is said to have kept two studios, one for the morning light and one for the afternoon⟦1⟧.

Twachtman spent his last summers at the Harbor View Hotel in East Gloucester, painting the boats and wharves. His view of the hotel from the end of its pier was on his easel when he died there in August 1902⟦0⟧; Duveneck had been painting beside him only days before⟦1⟧. Through his pupil Leon Kroll, his influence reached Edward Hopper⟦2⟧.

Philadelphia’s great portraitist, and from 1895 to 1915 the first woman to teach at the Pennsylvania Academy, Beaux first came with her family in the mid-1880s and stayed at the Fairview Inn. Fame cost her privacy, so in 1903 she rented a cottage on Eastern Point and by 1906 had built Green Alley, her house and studio there. Her 1930 memoir, ⟦0⟧Background with Figures⟦1⟧, credits her family for planting what grew for her in Gloucester⟦2⟧.

Prendergast made more than 2,300 paintings and drawings, many of them New England beaches. In his Gloucester watercolors a loose pencil sketch guided rather than governed the brush: he changed his mind as he went, so that figures turned into rocks, and he sharpened edges with touches of pastel⟦0⟧.

Twachtman’s student at the Art Students League, Kroll found Cézanne in Paris and showed at the 1913 Armory Show⟦0⟧. He brought Edward Hopper to Gloucester in 1912⟦1⟧. From the 1930s he and his wife Genevieve summered at Folly Cove near Halibut Point, bought a house there in 1944, and counted Paul Manship, Walker Hancock and Virginia Lee Burton among their friends⟦2⟧. He also painted the Bass Rocks footbridge that Rothko later sketched⟦3⟧.

Hopper’s 1912 oils are solid and dark. In 1923 he courted Josephine Nivison here and, at her urging, took up watercolor; the next summer the newlyweds came back on an extended honeymoon, exploring by foot and streetcar⟦0⟧. By 1928 his Gloucester sales had bought him a car⟦1⟧. The ⟦2⟧Hopper trail⟦3⟧ finds twelve of his subjects.

After the 1913 Armory Show, the Ashcan painter went looking for new ground. His friend Charles Winter urged Gloucester, and from 1914 Sloan rented a little red cottage at the head of Rocky Neck for five summers. It filled with painters: Stuart Davis, Agnes Richmond, Charles and Alice Beach Winter, Paul Cornoyer, Paul Tietjens. The Cape Ann Museum owns eight of his Gloucester pictures⟦0⟧. The cottage still stands at 252 East Main Street⟦1⟧.

Sloan invited him in 1915, and Davis called Gloucester “the place I had been looking for”. He came back for many summers through 1934, drawn to the schooners and the clutter of the docks. In time he left the easel and canvases behind and went out with only a sketchbook and pen, and in Gloucester he began combining several views and moments in one picture, the Cubist idea that runs through his later work⟦0⟧.

In 1919 Demuth painted Gloucester’s masts, roofs and church towers outdoors, cutting them into the ruled, transparent planes that became Precisionism⟦0⟧. The RISD Museum’s ⟦1⟧Gloucester⟦2⟧ has released its image to the public domain⟦3⟧.

Hartley shunned the busy waterfront for Dogtown, the abandoned colonial settlement in the middle of Cape Ann, which he thought looked like a cross between Easter Island and Stonehenge. He wrote poems on the backs of some of the paintings⟦0⟧. In 1931 he boarded with the Wilkens family at 9 Rocky Neck Avenue, treating the summer as a warm-up for a Guggenheim-funded trip to Mexico⟦1⟧.

Bernstein first came in 1916 on a friend’s advice. Meyerowitz, born in Russia, had paid for his training by singing in the Metropolitan Opera; the two met through the People’s Art Guild and married in 1919⟦0⟧. In the early 1920s Ellen Day Hale lent them a Folly Cove cottage, and Bernstein’s ⟦1⟧New England Ladies⟦2⟧ (1925) records an elderberry-wine party there, guest by guest⟦3⟧. Meyerowitz’s ⟦4⟧Gloucester Humoresque⟦5⟧ marks the founding in 1922 of the North Shore Arts Association, which juried its shows, and the Gloucester Society of Artists, which proudly did not⟦6⟧.

Avery’s first Gloucester pictures still owe something to Twachtman; over his Cape Ann summers the forms flattened and the color took over. He held to one rule: simplify anything, invent nothing. In 1932 he brought his young friends Gottlieb, Rothko and Barnett Newman⟦0⟧. The museum dates his first visit to 1920; the Rocky Neck Art Colony says 1921⟦1⟧.

In 1934 Rothko and his wife, Edith Sachar, reached Gloucester before the Gottliebs and took the Calder Street house the Gottliebs had wanted⟦0⟧. He painted the fish wharfs from Banner Hill, the bathers, and his friends at handball; the catalogue raisonné lists 38 Gloucester sheets⟦1⟧. In 1965 he gave the memorial address for Avery, calling him above all a great poet⟦2⟧. The ⟦3⟧Rothko trail⟦4⟧ has every sheet you can see.
Gruppé opened the Gloucester School of Art on Rocky Neck in 1929 and ran it for thirty years. His advice to students: think of a shape first, not of a horse or a tree or a boat⟦0⟧.

A Hans Hofmann student and a founder of New York’s Jane Street Gallery, Blaine first came in 1943 and rented Rocky Neck studios in 1954 and 1958. ⟦0⟧Time⟦1⟧ named her one of five leading women artists in America in 1957. Two years later polio left her in a wheelchair; she learned to paint again, and from 1974 summered at Eudora Cottage in East Gloucester, painting her garden, the ledges and the harbor⟦2⟧.
More lives are on the ⟦0⟧Women of Cape Ann trail⟦1⟧ (Martha Walter, Sally Michel Avery, Jane Peterson, Virginia Lee Burton) and the ⟦2⟧photographers page⟦3⟧.

Which great American painters worked in Gloucester and on Cape Ann, Massachusetts, and where their pictures hang today

From Fitz Henry Lane’s harbor of the 1840s to Rothko’s wharfs and Nell Blaine’s Rocky Neck, Gloucester and Cape Ann drew painters for more than a hundred years. This brief catalogues their pictures, says where each one hangs, and maps nine places where you can stand where they stood.

Who painted Gloucester and Cape Ann, and when
Each bar runs from a painter’s earliest to latest dated work in this brief; undated works are left out. Darker bars mark the painters of the nine mapped sites.

Gloucester’s own Fitz Henry Lane painted his harbor from the 1840s until his death in 1865, with Mary Blood Mellen working beside him. Winslow Homer spent the summers of 1873 and 1880 here; his oils are at the National Gallery of Art and the Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art, and his watercolors at the Met, the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, the Philadelphia Museum of Art, Princeton and elsewhere.⟦0⟧ Childe Hassam’s harbor views of about 1899 are at the Norton Museum of Art and the Newark Museum, and his 1918–19 pictures at the Met, PAFA and the Harn.

Hunt and Bricher came in the 1870s; Twachtman, Metcalf, Duveneck, Beaux and Prendergast around the turn of the century; then Hopper, Sloan, Davis, Demuth and Hartley, Milton Avery and the young Mark Rothko and Adolph Gottlieb, and the Rocky Neck and Rockport colonies. This brief catalogues 131 of their Gloucester and Cape Ann works, by 35 painters, nearly all in 48 public collections. A November 2026 update adds sixteen more, by Mary Blood Mellen, Charles Demuth, Mark Rothko, Theresa Bernstein, Nell Blaine, Max Kuehne and Earl Horter.

Born in Gloucester in 1804, Lane painted its harbor, Ten Pound Island, Stage Fort, Eastern Point and Norman's Woe for two decades. The Cape Ann Museum holds the largest group of his pictures; it has no stable object pages, so its holdings are cited through its own catalogue raisonné, ⟦0⟧Fitz Henry Lane Online⟦1⟧.⟦2⟧ The NGA's 2025.89 numbers mark a recent gift, and its links may change. Before painting full time he worked in lithography shops; the Cape Ann Museum also holds his first known work, a watercolor of 1830, about 100 drawings and all three of his lithographed views of Gloucester.⟦3⟧ From the mid-1850s Mary Blood Mellen worked beside him, free to copy his drawings and at times his canvases; one painting, ⟦4⟧Coast of Maine⟦5⟧, bears both their signatures.

Homer spent summer 1873 in Gloucester at the Atlantic House, and summer 1880 on Ten Pound Island with the lighthouse keeper, Oliver Merrill. He did not work there again (⟦0⟧MFA Boston, “When Homer Went to Gloucester”⟦1⟧).⟦2⟧ The NGA's Gallery M68 hangs ⟦3⟧“Dad's Coming!”⟦4⟧ and ⟦5⟧Breezing Up⟦6⟧ side by side. His 1880 ⟦7⟧Eastern Point Light⟦8⟧ is Gloucester's lighthouse; his better-known ⟦9⟧Eastern Point⟦10⟧ of 1900 is Prouts Neck, Maine. In Gloucester he left the studio to work outdoors, and there he made himself a master of watercolor, almost to the exclusion of oil.

Hunt spent summer 1877 at Magnolia, at Gloucester's western edge. He painted his ⟦0⟧Gloucester Harbor⟦1⟧ outdoors in a single afternoon at Kettle Cove, which the MFA calls “a fishing village in Gloucester”; Kettle Cove sits on the Magnolia–Manchester line.⟦2⟧⟦3⟧ Bricher worked the beaches of Cape Ann in the mid-1870s. Hunt had brought the ideas of the French Barbizon painters to Boston, taught John La Farge and William and Henry James, and from 1868 opened his classes to women. His Magnolia studio drew other painters to Cape Ann, and it was probably through him that Frank Duveneck first heard of it.

Hassam's harbor views date from about 1899; the church, street and hilltop pictures, and his ⟦0⟧Inner Harbor, Gloucester⟦1⟧ prints, from 1918–19 and after. The Norton's ⟦2⟧Gloucester Harbor⟦3⟧ is the picture most often reproduced.

Twachtman spent his last three summers in Gloucester, painting the harbor from East Gloucester. His catalogue raisonné dates ⟦0⟧Fishing Boats at Gloucester⟦1⟧ to about 1900 (OP.1420) and lists Gloucester oils in at least six museums.⟦2⟧ That last summer he lived in a small cottage studio over the water at the Harbor View Hotel; Duveneck was painting beside him only days before his sudden death in August 1902.⟦3⟧⟦4⟧ His pupil Leon Kroll would bring Edward Hopper to Gloucester in 1912.

Prendergast painted Gloucester from about 1907 into the early 1920s: the harbor from the hills of East Gloucester, Bass Rocks and the beaches and bathhouses of Annisquam. The largest group is at the Williams College Museum of Art, from the artist's family. He sketched lightly in pencil and then let the watercolor wander from it, turning figures into rocks and sharpening edges with touches of pastel.

Painters of the 1880s to 1910s who left Gloucester and Cape Ann pictures in public collections: Willard Metcalf and Frank Duveneck, who summered in East Gloucester; Cecilia Beaux, who built her house and studio there; H. Bolton Jones and Sarah Wyman Whitman. Sanford Gifford’s sketches of 1864–65 at Manchester-by-the-Sea, on Cape Ann’s southwest shore, are included too. Duveneck brought a summer class from Boston and Cincinnati in 1890, apparently the first large class of its kind in town, and came back for about fifteen summers; he is said to have kept two studios, one for the morning light and one for the afternoon.⟦0⟧⟦1⟧ Beaux, the first woman to teach at the Pennsylvania Academy, first came with her family in the mid-1880s and by 1906 had built Green Alley on Eastern Point.

Hopper painted Gloucester in 1912 and again in 1923–28; Brooklyn bought six of his Gloucester watercolors in 1923.⟦0⟧ Sloan summered there in 1914–18; Davis returned from 1915 into the 1930s; Hartley painted Dogtown Common in 1931 and 1934; Avery summered in Gloucester most years from 1920 to 1945.⟦1⟧ To stay clear of copyright questions, these later works are listed with links to each museum's own image rather than reproduced. Hopper first came with his friend Leon Kroll, and in 1923 took up watercolor at the urging of Josephine Nivison, whom he married the next year.⟦2⟧ Sloan came on the advice of Charles Winter and in 1915 invited Stuart Davis, who called Gloucester the place he had been looking for.⟦3⟧⟦4⟧ Hartley kept away from the waterfront and walked into Dogtown, which he likened to Easter Island and Stonehenge.

From the 1910s Rocky Neck in East Gloucester, and Rockport across the cape, drew working colonies of painters. The Rockport Art Association holds many of their pictures but has no searchable online catalogue.⟦0⟧ These are the colony works confirmed in other public collections. Emile Gruppé opened the Gloucester School of Art on Rocky Neck in 1929 and ran it for thirty years.⟦1⟧ In 1922 the North Shore Arts Association, which juried its shows, and the Gloucester Society of Artists, which refused juries, were founded half a mile apart on Eastern Point Road.

Sixteen works added after further research. ⟦0⟧Mary Blood Mellen⟦1⟧, Lane’s student and collaborator in the 1850s, is now credited with pictures once given to Lane. ⟦2⟧Charles Demuth⟦3⟧ spent the summer of 1919 in Gloucester, breaking its wharves and houses into the faceted planes that became Precisionism. ⟦4⟧Mark Rothko⟦5⟧ and ⟦6⟧Adolph Gottlieb⟦7⟧ came at Milton Avery’s invitation in the early 1930s; in the summer of 1934 Rothko rented a house on Calder Street in East Gloucester and painted the fish wharfs of the Inner Harbor, the beach and his friends at handball. The Rothko catalogue raisonné lists 38 Gloucester works on paper, 24 of them in public collections; the Rothko trail on the website lists them all. The Cape Ann Museum’s 2026 exhibition ⟦8⟧Avery, Gottlieb & Rothko: By the Sea⟦9⟧ told that story and is at the Phillips Collection, Washington, from October 24, 2026, to January 24, 2027; in August 2026 Christopher Rothko gave the museum one of his father’s Gloucester watercolors. ⟦10⟧Theresa Bernstein⟦11⟧ painted Gloucester from 1916 until nearly the end of her 111 years, and ⟦12⟧Nell Blaine⟦13⟧ worked on Rocky Neck in the 1950s and summered in East Gloucester from 1974 to 1996. Max Kuehne’s and Earl Horter’s Gloucester oils come from the Whitney’s open collection data. The two Demuths and the Mellen are public domain and are reproduced here; the later works are in copyright and are listed with links to each museum’s own image.

A minister’s wife from Sterling, Massachusetts, Mellen came into Fitz Henry Lane’s world after her brother-in-law took the Universalist pulpit in Gloucester in 1855. By the middle of the decade she was working beside Lane, with free use of his drawings and at times his canvases…
Hopper came to Gloucester in 1912 with his friend Leon Kroll, and again in the summers of 1923, 1924, 1926 and 1928, mostly painting houses in watercolor. Twelve of his subjects can still be found.

In August 2026 Christopher Rothko gave the museum his father’s ⟦0⟧Untitled (wharf, Gloucester, Massachusetts)⟦1⟧ of 1934, the first Rothko in its collection. It shows the salt-fish sheds of the Reed and Gamage wharfs near Smith Cove, painted from Banner Hill.

Avery painted the crowd watching the total solar eclipse of 1932 at Good Harbor. Two years later the friends met here daily: Edith Rothko remembered that they would “go swimming and play handball,” and Rothko painted the game.

Smith Cove was the center of Gloucester’s gill-net fishing. Rothko painted its wharfs again and again in 1934: the Reed and Gamage salt-fish sheds with a water tank on the roof, and rows of fish flakes covered with white cloths to keep the sun off the fillets; fishermen among the gill-net reels on a wharf…

The ridge above Smith Cove, where the Impressionists painted. Rothko painted the Reed and Gamage wharfs from Banner Hill, and Gottlieb sketched them from a similar spot, possibly beside him. The hilltop is private; look from the road.
